paragraphs.text: The Multiverse is the primary setting of Magic: The Gathering . It is composed of a finite but very large number of planes of existence , which are separated by the Blind Eternities and connected by Omenpaths . At the border of the known Multiverse lies the Edge , seperated from the Blind Eternities by a physical barrier called the Chaos Wall .

Most sets and stories take place on specific planes, or worlds. Every plane has its own unique denizens, magic, and metaphysics. Most planes have a theme derived from history, mythology, or popular culture; for example, Theros is inspired by ancient Greece, and Innistrad by Gothic horror.

The total number of planes is unknown. Urza believed that the number was finite, but too large to be counted in the combined lifetimes of every being in existence. Other sources have described the Multiverse as "boundless", or claimed that the planes are "countless" or possibly infinite.

Following the New Phyrexian Invasion , portals known as Omenpaths began to open between planes. Until then, only Planeswalkers were capable of interplanar travel, and few non-Planeswalkers were even aware of the existence of other planes. Describing the Omenpaths as "trans-planar arteries", the stitcher Geralf Cecani pondered the effects of planar travel on non-Planeswalkers; he believed that every plane of existence has its own rules of magic and that every magic user over time will have their magic adapt itself to the natural rules of the new plane.
The Blind Eternities are chaotic aether maelstrom which separate the planes of existence. Only Planeswalkers and unique beings such as the Eldrazi are capable of traversing them.
The Edge , also called the Edge of Eternity, is a ring-shaped universe bordering the Multiverse. It is outside the Multiverse proper, separated from it by a border known as the Chaos Wall .

The inhabitants of the Edge are generally not aware of the Multiverse and the planes within it, although the Drix have posited the existence of different "lamellae of creation", or realities, past the Chaos Wall, which may or may not refer to the planes. When a vessel makes use of faster-than-light travel , it plunges into the parallel lamellae behind the Chaos Wall—"the Eternities" or "Weft"—and then reemerges at its destination point.

The exact structure of the Multiverse is unknown, although some characters have great insight into it. Within the mind of Loot there is a real-time map of the entire Multiverse: each plane appears as a point of light, and within those points of light, there are further points representing Omenpaths to other planes. When viewing the map in Loot's mind, planes can be seen being born from the World Tree . Planes can also be seen dissolving into "black holes of aether."
Even after losing her spark, the Wanderer is still more aware of the planes and how they fit together and function than anyone else in the Multiverse, except for maybe Loot .

The "Nexus of the Multiverse" is a plane in the center of the Multiverse with a great influence on other planes. The world of Dominaria is known to have been the Nexus. Since the plane had only been in existence for a finite amount of time, and older planes are known (such as Equilor ), this was probably not always the case. Dominaria stopped being the Nexus of the Multiverse after the Mending . During the New Phyrexian Invasion , while Wrenn was connected to the Multiverse through Realmbreaker , she claimed to be "the nexus of all that is", possibly referring to the Nexus of the Multiverse.

Being a Nexus is probably connected with a large amount of mana lines flowing into it from other planes. That lets it quickly regenerate its supplies of mana and most likely is a way of how it affects other planes. Its collapse can destroy the time stream —an abrupt end of the Multiverse's existence and the near-infinite amount of its planes.

Following the New Phyrexian Invasion , Omenpaths began opening across the Multiverse. Niv-Mizzet recognized their patterns as a significant threat to his plane and devised a plan to regulate their access in a way to position Ravnica as a locus of the Multiverse.

Richard Garfield , the creator of Magic: The Gathering , conceived of "an infinite system of planes through which wizards travel in search of resources to fuel their magic" to match the trading card game 's modular nature. This provided a unified and coherent setting, while still leaving room for future expansions with almost any flavor .

As initially conceived, the Multiverse was named Dominia (doh-MIN-ee-uh ) Wizards of the Coast used this branding in the Encyclopedia Dominia and the Continuity team was, for a period, called "Dominia Continuity". The similarity between the name of the Multiverse and the name of the primary plane featured in sets (" Dominaria ") caused confusion for both players and developers. Early lore sources justified the similarity by describing the latter as a portmanteau of "Dominia" and "aria", meaning "Song of Dominia", but newer stories gave alternative derivations for the name of the plane. By 2007, the name "Dominia" had been officially retired from use. The Multiverse at large no longer has a name.

Some products don't use the Multiverse as a setting. Dungeons & Dragons and Universes Beyond sets feature separate intellectual properties which don't interact with Magic canon . Un-sets take place in the Un-iverse , a separate multiverse apart from the main continuity.
The Multiverse interacted with an alternate reality, maybe a parallel multiverse, in the Planar Chaos storyline.
Earth is not a part of the Multiverse. This is because R&D doesn't want to tell stories about planeswalkers visiting Earth or being from Earth.

Gavin Verhey used Earth as a non-canon plane for Wizards of the Coast in the Unknown Event at MagicCon Minneapolis 2023 . As the test cards in the event are designed to be humorous or silly, it is not considered a change in position on the use of Earth as a plane. Earth is used as an official plane type in the Doctor Who Commander decks Planechase cards, but they are a part of the Universes Beyond model. The setting of Portal Three Kingdoms closely resembles historic Earth, but was retroactively considered to be a parallel plane and later established as entirely separate from the Multiverse, similar to Universes Beyond sets.
